_premise: PREMISE (owner correction, Aug 28 2026): there is no philosophically good or bad company. Natural systems have no morality; they are either in balance or accumulating an imbalance that is eventually corrected, by regulation, substitution, exhaustion or collapse. The engine scores one mechanical question: does this business move its system toward equilibrium (closing loops, lowering energy and cost per useful outcome, distributing rather than concentrating, repairing rather than depleting) or does it earn by holding the system out of balance, which is a liability with a delay on it. The hard-rejection list is not a morality list, each entry names a model whose revenue REQUIRES sustained imbalance. Alignment with balance indicates the direction a system will push over decades; it does not by itself indicate the company will survive to capture it, which is why survivability, moat and expansion are scored separately.
_clock: CLOCK PRINCIPLE (owner correction, Aug 28 2026): time is relative to the correcting system, not the observer. An imbalance corrects on the clock of whatever mechanism does the correcting: substitution and reimbursement in months to a few years; regulation, litigation and technology displacement in years to a decade; infrastructure and demographic cycles over decades; soil, aquifers, oceans and climate over centuries. A system can therefore sit out of balance for an entire human investing life while barely registering on the clock of the thing that will correct it. Consequences for scoring: (1) direction without timing is not investable, so expansion_signal and survivability are the framework's clock instruments and must not be treated as secondary; (2) a name aligned with a centuries-scale correction and no near-term momentum should score low on expansion_signal, not be rewarded for being 'right'; (3) the framework's claim is only that WHEN a correction lands it lands on the businesses holding the system out of balance, while those helping it settle absorb the released demand. It makes no claim about when. Which clock is being bet on is the owner's decision, not the algorithm's.
_rubric: Six measures on one 100 point scale. A the stock (20), B the flow (25), C the loop (20, split 12 sign and 8 coupling), D growth pattern (15, split replication, contact inhibition and clean exit), E buffer (10), F clock (10, split time constant and current momentum). Survivability is a gate, not a score: a company that cannot fund itself to the horizon in F is excluded rather than ranked lower. Jurisdiction penalties apply after the total.

_calibration.shift: Every name was re-scored. The mean fell 7.0 points and 42 of 53 names moved down. The correlation between the old score and the new one is 0.07, so this is not the same ranking shifted; it is a different measurement.
_calibration.bands_not_moved: Tier bands were deliberately left at 80 / 74 / 69 / 65. Moving them down to keep 29 names in Tier 1 would have reproduced the previous answer by arithmetic. Tier 1 now holds 12 names, 11 of them investable. If only 11 clear the bar, 11 clear the bar.
_calibration.rail_cluster_kept: Four rail names fell hardest (UNP -30, CP -27, CNI -18, WAB -16). This was checked as a possible rubric artifact and kept as a real result. The moat deduction is evidence backed rather than structural: rail moves a ton of freight roughly 480 miles per gallon against about 145 for trucks, and rail's modal share against trucking still has not moved. A position that captures that advantage as captive shipper margin instead of passing it through as volume is throttling the correction it would otherwise drive. The replication score is likewise the observed pattern: all three Class I railroads are currently growing by merger, not by copying a unit.
_calibration.known_property: The scorecard is deliberately hostile to long clock infrastructure. Measure F says so in the rubric: being right about the imbalance and wrong about the clock is indistinguishable from being wrong. Every name with a decades clock sits at F_clock 3 of 6. This is a designed property, not a defect, and it is the single largest reason the rail and utility shaped businesses rank lower than they did.
_calibration.measure_f_is_near_constant: Within these 53 finalists, F_clock spans only 3 to 5 of 6 and F_now spans 2 to 4 of 4, correlating -0.13 with the total. Measure F did its discriminating upstream, in the six round screen, where names with no dated momentum were already cut. It separates the universe, not the finalists.
_calibration.inter_rater_check: Comparable businesses scored by different researchers landed within 5 to 10 points of each other: infection control spread 5, construction attachments 5, molecular diagnostics 9, cardiac monitoring 10. Rail spread 15, and that spread traces to real differences, since Wabtec sells a replicable retrofit while the railroads own corridors.

_gate_rule: Survivability gate, checked before scoring: under 12 months runway with no committed financing, three year dilution above 25 percent, a pending buyout, or going concern doubt. Two names fail: Butterfly Network on roughly 28 percent three year dilution despite scoring 80, and Demand Works on 34.8 percent dilution in one year. A gate failure is not a judgment about the business.

_audit_exemptions._premise: contains the phrase it rejects. The sentence reads that there is no philosophically good or bad company. A word-match audit will flag it; the negation is the point.
